title: Hiring & Building an AI Engineering Team: Dr. Bryan Bischof

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is about building AI engineering teams and centralized AI platform teams that enable product teams, fitting the platform and developer tooling frame. The talk addresses AI engineering practices at Hex, a developer tools company, focusing on team building for developer platforms. The talk covers team formation and product development practices across early, middle, and late company stages. The content is accessible to practitioners but most actionable for engineering leaders managing AI teams. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. All evidence anchors are graded 'said_in_transcript' representing the speaker's personal experience and opinions.

summary:
Dr. Bryan Bischof, Head of AI at Hex, presents on hiring and building AI engineering teams at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. Hex is described as a data science platform akin to a powerful Jupyter notebook. Bryan has 12 years in data science/ML and has been building AI capabilities at Hex for about 1.5 years. His tweet about hiring his first AI engineer was one inspiration for the 'rise of the AI engineer' blog post.

His first AI engineer job posting sought a senior SWE or MLE for greenfield work, explicitly excluding ML researchers wanting to publish at ICLR, requiring production AI experience, MLOps knowledge, and comfort in Python and TypeScript. Hiring needs vary by company stage: early needs data profiles and product competency; middle adds infra and design (the most under-invested area); later adds MLEs for fine-tuning and retrieval. He defines data profiles as data scientists and analysts skilled at examining distributions and product analytics.

He warns the mythical man month is magnified in AI, and the hiring schedule should reflect the development schedule: ship early product, build evals, get user feedback, iterate. Data must come earlier than in traditional product engineering. His hiring thesis by role: full-stack engineers integrate LLM providers and build minimum infrastructure; data scientists own evaluation quality and user data; product people must understand jobs to be done; designers are needed because AI products look 'clownish'; MLEs push beyond commodity intelligence.

For 'who,' attributes covarying with impact include data intuition, product mindedness, and urgency. He strongly opposes leetcode interviews. His hiring loop includes a take-home data cleaning exercise—a clustering problem with no objectively correct clusters—giving candidates several days, followed by a live feedback session. He also values a product design interview where candidates design a physical product with the design team. He looks for candidates forming real opinions about AI products, not just riding the wave.

Beyond hiring, his strongest advice is to work directly with domain experts—AI capabilities should be modeled after expert interactions. He talks to Hex data scientists weekly without exception. On upskilling existing teams, he advocates a centralized AI platform team whose charter is enabling product teams to move fast, referencing the Stitch Fix data platform model, while noting Netflix takes a different divergent approach. On security, he believes it generally lies outside the AI team, though engineers should be security-savvy, and acknowledges regulated environments may benefit from embedding security professionals in product teams.

In a final Q&A, Bryan clarifies that all three core attributes—data intuition, product mindedness, and urgency—need at least a kernel present to be developable; zero on any of them scares him. He then reveals one latent feature he had not previously mentioned: curiosity, which he has never personally successfully trained and considers a big, powerful feature in his model.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Explicitly exclude ML researchers wanting to publish papers from AI engineer job postings if that is not what you need—save everyone's time.
Hiring depends on company stage: early needs data profiles and product competency; middle adds infra and design (most under-invested); later adds MLEs for fine-tuning and retrieval.
The mythical man month is especially dangerous in AI—hiring more people does not accelerate early AI products that change every three months.
Attributes covarying with impact: data intuition, product mindedness, and urgency. Stop using leetcode—use data cleaning take-homes and product design interviews instead.
Curiosity is the one attribute Bryan has never successfully trained, making it non-negotiable. All three core attributes need at least a kernel present; zero on any scares him.
Work directly with domain experts—AI capabilities should be modeled after interactions with experts. This is the most important success factor beyond hiring.
For upskilling existing teams, establish a centralized AI platform team so product teams don't independently rebuild LLM integrations, prompt infrastructure, and evaluation systems.

Security responsibility generally lies outside the AI team, though engineers should be security-savvy; regulated environments may benefit from embedding security professionals directly in product teams.

sections.title: Introduction and Credentials
sections.summary: Bryan introduces Hex as a data science platform, shares his 12-year background, and claims his tweet about hiring his first AI engineer inspired the 'rise of the AI engineer' blog post.

sections.title: First AI Engineer Job Posting
sections.summary: Details the original job posting: senior SWE or MLE for greenfield work, explicitly excluding ML researchers wanting ICLR publications, seeking production AI experience, MLOps knowledge, and comfort in Python and TypeScript.

sections.title: When to Hire Across Company Stages
sections.summary: Hiring needs vary by stage: early needs data profiles and product competency; middle needs infra, data profiles, and design (most under-invested); later needs scaled infra and MLEs for fine-tuning and retrieval. Defines data profiles as data scientists and analysts who examine distributions and product analytics.

sections.title: Mythical Man Month and Development Schedule
sections.summary: Warns the mythical man month is magnified in AI. The hiring schedule must reflect the development schedule: early product, then evals, then user feedback, then iterate. Data needs to come earlier than in traditional engineering. References a Hex paper on building LLMs.

sections.title: Why Hire: Hiring Thesis by Role
sections.summary: Presents hiring thesis for each role: full-stack engineers integrate LLM providers and build minimum infra; data scientists own evaluation quality and user data; product people must understand jobs to be done; designers address the 'clownish' state of current AI products; MLEs push beyond commodity intelligence.

sections.title: Who and How to Hire
sections.summary: Impact-covarying attributes: data intuition, product mindedness, urgency. Strongly opposes leetcode interviews. His hiring loop uses a data cleaning take-home and a coding challenge most would find easy, testing real job skills.

sections.title: Hiring Loop Details and Product Design Interview
sections.summary: Expands on the coding challenge investment and introduces Hex's product design interview. Looks for candidates forming real opinions about AI products, not just riding the wave. Example of hiring an AI engineer whose blog post about AI design patterns demonstrated deep awareness.

sections.title: AI Leader GPT and Working with Domain Experts
sections.summary: AI leader GPT chatbot advises working with experts. Bryan emphasizes domain expert collaboration as the most important factor beyond hiring. AI capabilities should be modeled after expert interactions; customer support bots need customer support people using them daily. He talks to Hex data scientists weekly without exception.

sections.title: Q&A: Data Intuition Interview Process
sections.summary: Details the take-home data intuition assessment: a clustering problem with no objectively correct clusters, given several days to complete, followed by a live feedback session. Feedback serves as mutual evaluation—candidates learn what working with Bryan is like, and he learns how they handle feedback. Red flag: over-scoping work; green flag: right-scoping or justifying simplicity.

sections.title: Q&A: Security, Upskilling, and Centralized Platform Teams
sections.summary: On security, Bryan believes it generally lies outside the AI team but engineers should be security-savvy; an audience member from a national laboratory advocates embedding security in product teams, which Bryan acknowledges for regulated environments. On upskilling existing teams, he advocates a centralized AI platform team modeled after Stitch Fix's data platform, with product teams interfacing like internal customers. Notes Netflix takes a divergent approach.

sections.title: Q&A: Non-Negotiable Attributes and Curiosity
sections.summary: When asked which attributes are non-negotiable vs. trainable, Bryan says all three core attributes (data intuition, product mindedness, urgency) need at least a kernel present to be developable—zero on any of them scares him. He then reveals one latent feature he had not previously mentioned: curiosity, which he has never personally successfully trained and considers a big, powerful feature in his model.
